about: A rewrite of the find and xargs tools in Rust, aiming to work the same as GNU findutils.

prs.title: A test keeps the stop-printing escape honest
prs.broken: The earlier fix that made find stop a print format at the stop escape had no test showing that the next action still runs for each file.
prs.changed: A new test runs two print actions and checks that the second still runs after the first stops early, matching GNU find.
prs.matters: The fix cannot quietly break later without a test failing.

prs.title: Date filters now need a file to be strictly newer
prs.broken: Asking find for files newer than a date also matched files with exactly that time, and dates before 1970 lost their minus sign, so a file from 1960 counted as newer than 1965.
prs.changed: A file now has to be strictly newer than the date, and times before 1970 compare the right way round.
prs.matters: Searches by date return the same files GNU find does.

prs.title: Date filters accept any date the date command understands
prs.broken: find's newer-than-a-date filters only took two fixed date layouts and read them as UTC. Common forms like yesterday, 1 day ago or an ISO date were rejected, and local times came out hours off.
prs.changed: find now reads these dates with the same parser the date and touch commands use, in local time.
prs.matters: Date searches that work with GNU find work here too, and land on the right hour.

prs.title: The -ls listing shows real disk usage and link targets
prs.broken: find's -ls listing showed every file's size rounded up as its disk usage, so a mostly empty sparse file looked huge, and symlinks did not show where they point.
prs.changed: It now shows the space a file really uses on disk, and each symlink is followed by an arrow and its target, like GNU find.
prs.matters: Scripts and people reading -ls output see the same columns as with GNU find.

prs.title: Dates in -printf pad the day with a space
prs.broken: The %t, %a and %c dates in find's -printf wrote early days of the month with a leading zero, like Jan 02, while GNU find writes Jan  2.
prs.changed: The day is now padded with a space, the classic format GNU find uses.
prs.matters: Output that scripts compare or parse matches GNU find.

prs.title: \c in -printf stops the output
prs.broken: GNU find's manual says \c in a -printf format stops printing right there. Here it only flushed the output, and the rest of the format was still printed.
prs.changed: Printing now stops at \c. Later actions on the same file still run, as in GNU find.
prs.matters: Scripts that use \c to cut a line short get the same output as with GNU find.

prs.title: xargs splits arguments only at spaces, tabs and newlines
prs.broken: xargs also split arguments at carriage returns and form feeds. A file with Windows line endings lost the carriage return at the end of each line's last word.
prs.changed: Only spaces, tabs and newlines separate arguments now. Other control characters stay inside the word, as in GNU xargs.
prs.matters: Input with Windows line endings or other control characters gives the same arguments as with GNU xargs.

prs.title: xargs -I reads input lines like GNU
prs.broken: With -I, each input line went in raw: leading spaces stayed, blank lines still ran the command, quotes were kept and the end marker was ignored.
prs.changed: -I now skips leading blanks and blank lines, handles quotes like plain xargs, and stops at the end marker, keeping each line as one argument.
prs.matters: Scripts that feed lines to xargs -I get the same commands as on GNU systems.

prs.title: find -ls shows file times in your own time zone
prs.broken: find's -ls output showed modification times in UTC, so on most machines the time was off by hours compared to GNU find and ls.
prs.changed: The time is now shown in the local time zone, in both the Unix and Windows code.
prs.matters: File listings show the same times as every other tool on the machine.
